summary: Defines two PIM Join/Prune attributes for building multicast trees between LISP sites. They let a receiver site choose unicast or multicast underlay transport and convey the receiver ETR's RLOC address. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8059 adds two attributes to PIM Join/Prune messages used between LISP sites. One selects multicast or unicast delivery, and the other tells the root site which receiver locator to use.

subtitle: Two PIM Join/Prune attributes for selecting transport and reporting a receiver's LISP locator.

tldr.problem: A Join/Prune message between LISP sites did not say whether the receiver wanted multicast or unicast delivery, or which receiver locator should receive the flow.
tldr.mechanism: The Transport attribute selects multicast or unicast. The Receiver RLOC attribute carries the receiver ETR's routing locator to the root ITR's control plane.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8059 is Experimental and is updated by RFC 9798. It assigns attribute types 5 and 6 and transport values 0 and 1.

today: RFC 8059 is an Experimental specification and is updated by RFC 9798. Its text says it was published for examination, experimental implementation, and evaluation.

sections.title: The Information Missing from Join/Prune
sections.content:
When a multicast root and its receivers are in different Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) sites, an Egress Tunnel Router (ETR) sends a Join/Prune message to an Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR) at the root site.

The earlier message format identified the multicast state but did not state whether the receiver wanted an underlying multicast or unicast transport. It also did not necessarily identify the receiver ETR's preferred Routing Locator (RLOC), because the packet's outer source address can differ from that locator.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver needs to tell the root how it wants multicast data delivered and which locator should receive it. RFC 8059 adds fields for both choices.

sections.title: Attributes in a PIM Join/Prune Message
sections.content:
The attributes use the Type-Length-Value format defined for PIM Join/Prune attributes. They can be attached to an individual source. When the same attribute applies to many sources, RFC 8059 recommends the hierarchical scheme from RFC 7887.

LISP tunnel routers do not exchange PIM Hello messages, so there is no Hello option for negotiating support. The RFC assumes that systems supporting unicast head-end replication also support these attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: The new information is carried as typed attributes inside an existing Join/Prune message. One shared attribute can apply to several sources in the message.

sections.title: The Transport Attribute
sections.content:
The Transport attribute has type 5 and a one-octet value. Value 0 requests multicast, and value 1 requests unicast. The attribute's transitive bit must be zero.

An encoded address must not contain more than one Transport attribute. The root ITR must discard the affected Join/Prune sources if the attribute is duplicated or its value is unknown.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute contains one value: zero means multicast and one means unicast. A duplicate or unknown value makes the affected source information unusable.

sections.title: The Receiver RLOC Attribute
sections.content:
The Receiver RLOC attribute has type 6. Its value contains the address family followed by the receiver ETR's RLOC, the address on which that site wants to receive the unicast-encapsulated flow.

The attribute length must equal the RLOC address length plus one octet for the address-family field. The root ITR must discard affected sources if the attribute is duplicated, the address family is unknown, or the address length is wrong. The attribute does not itself add security to the PIM message.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver includes the locator it wants the root to use. The root ignores the affected source if the locator information is duplicated or invalid.

fields.name: E bit
fields.desc: Marks whether this is the last attribute.
